title: Renting an Allotment Plot
context: A caller enquires about renting a vegetable plot from a town council.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Good morning, Riverbank Town Council, allotments office. How can I help?

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Hello. I'd like to ask about renting a plot, please. A friend of mine has one and said there might be spaces.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: There are, as it happens. We've just had a few come free at the Millgate site. Can I take some details first?

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Of course.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Your full name?

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: It's Priya Anand. Anand is A-N-A-N-D.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: A-N-A-N-D. Thank you. And an address?

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Forty-two Weaver Street. That's in the Northfield area.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Forty-two Weaver Street. And a contact number?

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Zero seven eight one one, nine double-oh, three five four.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Let me read that back. Zero seven eight one one, nine hundred, three five four.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: That's right.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Now, the plots at Millgate come in two sizes. There's a full plot, which is about two hundred and fifty square metres, and a half plot at a hundred and twenty-five.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Which would you recommend? I've never done this before.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Honestly, the half plot. People take a full one, get overwhelmed by the digging, and give it up within a year. You can always move up later.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: That sounds sensible. I'll take a half plot then.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Good. The rent for a half plot is sixty-two pounds a year.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Is that payable monthly?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: No, it's a single annual payment, I'm afraid. There's also a one-off deposit of twenty pounds, which you get back when you leave, provided the plot is left clear.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Fine. What's actually provided on the site?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: There's water from standpipes along the main path, and a communal shed with tools you can borrow. We supply compost twice a year, in spring and autumn.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Do I need to bring my own lock?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Yes, for the gate. Everyone uses the same type — it's a combination lock, and we'll give you the code when you sign.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Are there any rules I should know about?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: A few. No bonfires between April and September. Dogs are allowed but must be kept on a lead. And the big one: no structures over two metres tall without written permission.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: What counts as a structure?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Sheds, greenhouses, anything permanent. A bean frame is fine.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Understood. When could I start?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: The next introduction session is on Saturday the ninth — no, sorry, I'm looking at last month's calendar. It's Saturday the sixteenth, at ten in the morning.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: The sixteenth. And how long does it take?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: About ninety minutes. You'll walk the site, meet the plot secretary and sign the agreement. Bring proof of address — a utility bill is easiest.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Can I bring a bank statement instead?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: That's fine, as long as it's from the last three months.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: Great. Is there anything else I should bring?

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: Just sensible footwear. The ground at Millgate is heavy clay and it holds the water after rain.

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: I'll remember that. Thank you very much for your help.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: You're welcome. I'll post the paperwork out today so you can read it beforehand.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.explanation: She spells it: A-N-A-N-D. Names are always either spelled out or repeated back — wait for the confirmation before committing.
"Forty-two Weaver Street", and the officer repeats it back. The number is already printed in the question, so only the street name is needed.

questions.sentence: A half plot measures about ___ square metres.
questions.explanation: A full plot is about 250 square metres and a half plot 125. The larger figure is said first and is the distractor. It is spoken as "a hundred and twenty-five", so either form is accepted.

questions.sentence: Annual rent for a half plot: £___
questions.explanation: "The rent for a half plot is sixty-two pounds a year." The twenty-pound deposit later in the call is a separate figure.
"A one-off deposit of twenty pounds, which you get back when you leave." Note "one-off" and "get back" — the words that separate a deposit from a rent.
The officer corrects himself: "Saturday the ninth — no, sorry ... It's Saturday the sixteenth." Corrections are a standard IELTS device; take the second date.
"About ninety minutes." Either the word or the figure is accepted, but "an hour and a half" would not match what was said.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.question: Why does the officer recommend a half plot?
options: It is the only size available
Beginners often find a full plot too much work
The soil is better on half plots
Full plots cost more to insure
questions.explanation: "People take a full one, get overwhelmed by the digging, and give it up within a year." The reason is the workload, and the officer never says a half plot is the only size.

questions.question: What must the caller supply herself?
questions.explanation: Tools are in the communal shed, compost is supplied twice a year and water comes from standpipes. Only the gate lock is the tenant's responsibility.

questions.question: What does the officer say about the ground at the site?
questions.explanation: "The ground at Millgate is heavy clay and it holds the water after rain." Holding water is the opposite of draining quickly, which is the option placed first to catch you.
